newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel set to build East Jerusalem settlement.
newsitem.headline: Israel set to build East Jerusalem settlement.

text.p: Israel was set to begin work on Tuesday on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, ringing the site with soldiers and vowing not to flinch from a showdown with Palestinians.

Construction supervisors at a staging point for earthmoving equipment about two kilometres (one mile) from the Har Homa site said surveyors would start work within hours. Bulldozers were loaded on to trucks for transfer to the hill, which Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Police chiefs decided to rush hundreds of reinforcements to Jerusalem in anticipation of a violent Palestinian backlash, officials said.
"We will not get down on our knees," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said.

Israel intends to build 6,500 homes for Jews at the hilltop site, another link in a concrete chain of apartment blocks that Israel has built to cement its hold on East Jerusalem and separate it from the rest of the West Bank.
National police chief Assaf Hefetz said police were preparing "for the ground to get hot".

The Palestinian Health Ministry declared a state of emergency at hospitals in self-ruled parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, an official at Ramallah hospital said. Measures, in force since Saturday, included sending some patients home.
There seemed to be little chance of a last-minute summit between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat which PLO officials said was conditioned on suspending the project.
Arafat spurned Netanyahu's appeals to meet him late on Monday, drawing Israeli accusations the Palestinian leader was trying to stoke already high tensions over the plan.
Dozens of Israeli soldiers in combat gear took up positions around the base of the pine-covered hill in anticipation of an outburst of Palestinian rage over the internationally condemned project.
"We are trying to do only one thing -- to have talks. If the Palestinian side is looking for a dialogue, we are also looking for one and not for confrontation," Naveh told Army Radio.
"But if the Palestinian side wants confrontation, we are also prepared for that," he said.
Netanyahu met senior ministers and security officials for 45 minutes to hear their security assessments. Near the windswept hill, Palestinian protesters sat in tents under a cloudy sky.
"The weather is very cold but the situation is very hot and tense as a result of the Israeli government's arrogance," said protester Salah Taamri, a member of the Palestinian legislature.
Israel said on Monday it had reinforced its troops in the West Bank and Gaza Strip to pre-empt any Palestinian violence.
The PLO wants East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war, as the capital of a Palestinian state. Israel regards all of Jerusalem as its "eternal capital".
The Israeli army declared an area between the hill and the West Bank town of Bethlehem a closed military area in a bid to ensure Palestinian protesters could not reach the site.
But Faisal al-Husseini, the PLO's top official in Jerusalem, and other Palestinians had by Tuesday pitched six tents near Har Homa, vowing to challenge the bulldozers.

"We are sleeping here to defend the land. We are determined to stay here until we believe that our objectives are reached," he said as about 15 Israeli soldiers huddled against the cold in a partially built abandoned house.

Last September, 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in clashes that erupted after Netanyahu punched another opening into an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem.
Arafat has called Israel's decision to build a "flagrant violation to what has been agreed upon".

Under the 1993 PLO-Israel peace accord the future of Jerusalem and the fate of Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza will be determined in "final status" talks that were supposed to have resumed on Monday and end in 1999.

The project was approved under Israel's previous Labour-led government, an advocate of trading land for peace. Labour protests over Netanyahu's plans are muted by what politicians say is a public consensus to retain all of Jerusalem.
